39.s: According to the World Food Summit, 1996, food security exists when all people, at all times, have physical and economic access to which of the following?

⚠ It does **not** mean food "**of their choice**" — a trap set in **APPSC G2 2017**; nor does it require supply only by government.
xa: The definition says **all people, at all times**, with **physical and economic access**.
Four dimensions: **availability, access (affordability), utilisation/absorption, stability**.
India achieved **national** food security (buffer stocks) without fully assuring **household** food security — hence **PDS** and **NFSA**.
39.tq: Use the precise official definition and reject the look-alike phrase ‘food of their choice’.

xa: **Availability** = production + imports + previous stocks.
**Absorption/utilisation** = the body's ability to use the food.
Price and quantity of exports are also **not** dimensions.

Capital inflows minus capital outflows plus errors and omissions
Exports and imports of goods only plus changes in foreign exchange reserves
Foreign direct investment plus portfolio investment minus external debt
75.x: The current-account balance equals exports minus imports of goods and services, plus net primary income and net secondary income.
xs: **Current account balance** = (exports − imports of **goods and services**) + **net primary income** + **net secondary income** — option **(1)**.
Capital flows and reserve changes (options 2, 3) belong to the capital account.
xa: APPSC-GS 2019 key: exports minus imports of goods **and services** + net unilateral transfers.
⚠ **BoT** = goods only; current account balance = goods **and services** + transfers.
A **CAD** must be financed by a capital account surplus or by drawing down reserves.
75.tq: Reconstruct the identity by adding goods, services, primary income and secondary income.

75.s: To reduce external vulnerability, which kind of external debt should be kept low?
xs: Safeguards: **adequate reserves (import cover)**, **low short-term debt**, **less reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows**
75.x: Safeguards: adequate reserves (import cover), low short-term debt, less reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows

75.s: Increased dependence on what raises a country's external vulnerability?
xs: US Fed hikes push **"hot money"** out of emerging markets.
75.x: US Fed hikes push "hot money" out of emerging markets.

75.s: FCNR(B) deposits and external commercial borrowings are viewed as what kind of inflows?
xs: **FCNR(B)** and **ECB** inflows are **temporary**;
75.x: FCNR(B) and ECB inflows are temporary;

75.s: FDI belongs to which BoP account?
xs: **FDI** is a capital movement and belongs to the **Capital Account**, with **foreign loans** and **portfolio investment**.
xa: **ECB** and **NRI deposits** (FCNR(B)) are capital account items.
75.x: FDI is a capital movement and belongs to the Capital Account, with foreign loans and portfolio investment.

75.s: Software services exports are recorded under which part of the BoP?
xs: **Software services exports** = **Current Account – services (invisibles)**; **crude oil imports** = **Current Account – merchandise trade**.
75.x: Software services exports = Current Account – services (invisibles); crude oil imports = Current Account – merchandise trade.

75.s: Crude oil imports are recorded under which part of the BoP?
xs: **Software services exports** = **Current Account – services (invisibles)**; **crude oil imports** = **Current Account – merchandise trade**.
75.x: Software services exports = Current Account – services (invisibles); crude oil imports = Current Account – merchandise trade.

75.s: For how many consecutive years did India record a current account surplus during the period 2001-02 to 2003-04?
75.x: India recorded a current account surplus for three consecutive years from 2001-02 to 2003-04.
xs: India ran a current account **surplus three years running** in **2001-02 to 2003-04** — option **(4)**, **three years**.
Such a run is **rare** in India's record.
xa: **Q4 2023-24** also saw a **surplus**, due to a **surge in services exports**.
CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13** (taper tantrum).
75.tq: Match the duration directly with the specified financial-year range.

75.s: India's current account recorded a surplus in which quarter?
The current account surplus in Q4 2023-24 was driven by what?
xs: It came from a **surge in services exports** (PYQ 2025).
75.x: It came from a surge in services exports (PYQ 2025).

75.s: India's current account deficit reached its peak of about 4.8% of GDP in:
o: 1990-91, during the balance of payments crisis
FY24, after the fall in imports
H1 FY26, after the US tariffs
75.x: The CAD peaked at about 4.8% of GDP in FY13, the taper tantrum period. In the 1990-91 crisis it was about 3.1-3.2% of GDP. FY24 saw a recovery, with a surplus in Q4, and H1 FY26 had a CAD of only 0.8% of GDP.
xs: India's CAD peaked at **4.8% of GDP** in **FY13**, around the **taper tantrum** — option **(2)**.
The **1990-91** crisis CAD was **3.1-3.2%**; **FY24** saw a recovery; **H1 FY26** CAD was only **0.8%**.
xa: In the **2013** taper tantrum **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
**Rangarajan Committee**: sustainable CAD about **1.6% of GDP**.
75.tq: CAD peak = 4.8% FY13; crisis year 1990-91 = ~3.1%.

75.s: During the 2013 taper tantrum, Morgan Stanley included India among the:
75.x: Morgan Stanley described India as one of the ‘Fragile Five’ during the 2013 taper tantrum because of external-sector vulnerability.
xs: During the **2013 taper tantrum**, **Morgan Stanley** named India one of the **"Fragile Five"** — option **(3)**.
The CAD then peaked at **4.8% of GDP** (**FY13**).
xa: In **May 2026** India's BoP was described as weak as the 2013 "Fragile Five" phase.
US Fed hikes → **hot money** exits → weaker rupee.
Safeguards: adequate reserves, low **short-term debt**.
75.tq: Recall the distinctive group label associated with the external shock.

75.s: What is a core function of the IMF?
xs: **RCF** = **concessional assistance** to **low-income countries**; IMF core function = **monitoring global and member economies**.
75.x: RCF = concessional assistance to low-income countries; IMF core function = monitoring global and member economies.

75.s: A global slowdown is what kind of cause of India's current account deficit?
xs: A **global slowdown** is a **cyclical** cause, not structural.
xa: Cyclical causes: **commodity shocks**, global slowdown, **rupee volatility**.
75.x: A global slowdown is a cyclical cause, not structural.

75.s: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed approximately what proportion of the merchandise deficit?
75.x: The record services surplus of $188.8 billion in FY25 financed about two-thirds of the merchandise deficit. Remittances also acted as a cushion.
xs: The record **services surplus** of **$188.8 bn** in **FY25** financed about **two-thirds** of the merchandise deficit — option **(4)**.
**Remittances** were the other **cushion**.
xa: **Software services** = largest part of the services surplus.
Net services in **Q1 FY27**: **$51.6 bn**.
Net **primary income** is an outflow — **$10.5 bn** in Q1 FY27.
75.tq: Identify the comparative proportion rather than treating the services surplus as full financing of the merchandise deficit.

75.s: India was estimated to be the world's largest recipient of remittances in FY25. What was the approximate amount of remittances and their share in India's GDP, respectively?
75.x: India received approximately $135.4 billion in remittances in FY25, equivalent to about 3.5% of its GDP.
xs: India, the **world's largest recipient**, got **$135.4 billion** (**3.5%** of GDP) in **FY25** — option **(1)**.
**$188.8 bn** is the **services surplus**; **$110.47 bn** and **$87.55 bn** are **workers' remittances** for FY26 and the year before.
xa: ⚠ **$135.4 bn** (FY25 total) vs **$110.47 bn** (FY26, workers' remittances — narrower measure).
Remittances exceed gross **FDI** inflows.
75.tq: Use the paired numerical figures and distinguish the annual estimate from other remittance measures.

75.s: Which one of the following best explains the significance of remittances in India's external sector?
o: They are counter-cyclical and do not create a debt burden or repayment obligation.
They are classified entirely as foreign direct investment inflows.
They can be received only through external commercial borrowings.
They are pro-cyclical and create a direct repayment obligation for the recipient country.
75.x: Remittances are counter-cyclical and do not create a repayment obligation, unlike debt-related flows such as ECBs or certain portfolio liabilities.
xs: Remittances are **counter-cyclical** and create **no debt burden / no repayment obligation** — option **(1)**.
Unlike **ECB/FPI** debt, they need no repayment; they are not FDI (they in fact **exceed gross FDI** inflows).
xa: Remittances = **$135.4 bn (3.5% of GDP)** in **FY25**.
Workers' remittances: **$110.47 bn** in **FY26**.
Critics warn of dependence on remittances + one-time deposit schemes instead of stable **FDI**.
75.tq: Apply the contrast between stable transfer inflows and debt-creating capital flows.

75.s: Which inflow is expected to support a self-sustaining capital surplus, unlike FCNR(B) and ECBs?
xs: **FDI** must drive a **self-sustaining capital surplus**
xa: FY26 **net FDI** was only **$6.9 bn**, down from **$44.0 bn** in **2020-21**.
75.x: FDI must drive a self-sustaining capital surplus

75.s: A capital-account transaction involving the purchase of foreign assets by residents is recorded as:
o: A current-account credit because assets are goods
A debit because foreign exchange flows out for acquiring the assets
A credit because foreign exchange enters the country
75.x: Purchase of foreign assets by residents is a capital-account debit. Conversely, sale of Indian assets to foreigners is recorded as a credit.
xs: **Purchase of foreign assets** by residents is a capital-account **debit** — foreign exchange flows out — option **(3)**.
**Sale of Indian assets to foreigners** is a **credit**.
xa: BoP is kept on **double-entry** bookkeeping, so it always balances in accounting terms.
Capital account items: **FDI**, **FPI/FII**, ADRs/GDRs, **ECB**, NRI deposits.
Surplus in one account = **deficit** in another.
75.tq: Follow the direction of the financial flow to distinguish a debit from a credit.

75.s: Adequate foreign-exchange reserves are a safeguard against external vulnerability by providing what?
xs: Safeguards: **adequate reserves (import cover)**, **low short-term debt**, **less reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows**
75.x: Safeguards: adequate reserves (import cover), low short-term debt, less reliance on volatile FPI and debt flows

75.s: How do increases in US Federal Reserve interest rates and a strong US dollar generally affect emerging markets such as India?
o: They automatically increase India’s net FDI
They raise US yields, attract hot money away from emerging markets and weaken the rupee
They reduce US yields and cause capital to flow into emerging markets
They eliminate exchange-rate volatility in emerging markets
75.x: US rate hikes and a strong dollar raise US yields, encouraging hot-money outflows from emerging markets and putting downward pressure on the rupee.
xs: **US Fed** rate hikes + a **strong dollar** → **higher US yields** → **"hot money" leaves emerging markets** → **weaker rupee** — option **(2)**.
So they do not lower US yields or raise India's FDI.
xa: **2013 taper tantrum**: India named one of the **"Fragile Five"**.
Safeguard: less reliance on volatile **FPI** and debt flows.
The rupee fell **~6.5%** against the dollar.
75.tq: Follow the capital-flow chain from interest-rate differential to exchange-rate pressure.

75.s: Which one of the following sets contains only expenditure-switching measures for correcting a Balance of Payments deficit?
o: Devaluation, import tariffs and export incentives
Reduced government spending, import quotas and higher interest rates
Fiscal restraint, monetary tightening and reduction in public expenditure
Higher interest rates, higher taxes and reduced government spending
75.x: A is correct: devaluation, import tariffs and export incentives all switch demand from foreign to domestic goods, so they are expenditure-switching measures. B is a mix (reduced government spending and higher interest rates are expenditure-reducing, though import quotas are switching), while C and D contain only expenditure-reducing fiscal and monetary measures.
xs: **Devaluation, import tariffs and export incentives** are all **expenditure-switching** — option **(1)**.
**Reduced government spending**, **higher interest rates** and **higher taxes** are **expenditure-reducing**, so options (2)–(4) are wrong.
xa: Other switching tools: **import quotas**, **import substitution**, **tourist incentives**.
Devaluation makes **home goods cheaper relative to foreign goods**.
⚠ Raising government spending is **NOT** a correction tool (PYQ 2025).
75.tq: Classify policies according to whether they switch demand or reduce total expenditure.

75.s: Which of the following is an expenditure-reducing measure used to correct a Balance of Payments deficit?
o: Tight monetary policy through higher interest rates
75.x: Tight monetary policy, including higher interest rates, reduces aggregate expenditure and imports. Devaluation, import substitution and export promotion are expenditure-switching measures.
xs: **Tight monetary policy** (deflation) through **higher interest rates** is **expenditure-reducing** — option **(2)**.
**Tourist incentives**, **import substitution** and **devaluation** are **expenditure-switching**.
xa: Other reducing tool: **tight fiscal policy** — cut government spending, raise taxes.
Financing tools: **foreign loans**, **IMF assistance**, encouraging FDI.
**Devaluation** = classic expenditure-switching policy.
75.tq: Identify the policy that reduces aggregate demand rather than redirecting it.

75.s: When a country’s foreign exchange reserves are insufficient to cover its Balance of Payments deficit, which institution may be approached as a lender of last resort in this context?
75.x: The International Monetary Fund may provide assistance when a country cannot cover its external deficit from its reserves and other available sources.
xs: If reserves cannot cover the deficit, the **International Monetary Fund (IMF)** is the **last resort** — option **(4)**.
The IMF lends to **correct BoP disequilibrium**; WTO, ILO and UNEP do not.
xa: IMF lending windows: **Stand-By Arrangement** + **Extended Fund Facility**.
India drew on the IMF in the **1991** crisis.
**SDRs** and **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF are part of India's reserves.
75.tq: Match the external-payments problem with the institution associated with balance-of-payments assistance.

75.s: The increase in import duty on gold, when used to reduce external pressure, is best classified as:
75.x: A higher import duty makes imported gold less attractive and helps switch demand towards domestic alternatives or away from imports. It is therefore an expenditure-switching measure.
xs: A **gold import duty hike** is an **expenditure-switching** step — option **(1)**.
Import tariffs/duties switch demand away from imports; it is not a monetary or transfer item.
xa: **May 2026**: the PM appealed to cut **gold** and **fuel** consumption as the **Iran** conflict raised prices.
Oil (**>80%** imported) and gold are **structural** causes of the CAD.
Other switching tools: **devaluation**, **export incentives**.
75.tq: Trace how an import duty changes the relative attractiveness of foreign goods.

75.s: Which of the following is NOT included among the components of India’s foreign exchange reserves?
75.x: India’s foreign exchange reserves include Foreign Currency Assets, gold, SDRs and the reserve position in the IMF. Fiscal deficit deposits are not a reserve component.
xs: **Fiscal deficit deposits** are not a reserve component — option **(2)**.
Reserves = **FCA**, **gold**, **SDRs** and the **Reserve Tranche Position** with the IMF.
xa: Reserves of **$701.4 bn** (**Jan 2026**) covered about **94%** of external debt.
A positive **overall BoP** adds to reserves.
**Reserve changes** are recorded in the capital account.
75.tq: Find the non-member of a standard reserve-components list.

75.s: Besides oil and gold dependence and low export competitiveness, which is a structural cause of India's CAD?
xs: **Structural** causes: **oil (>80% imported) and gold**, **low export competitiveness**, **savings-investment gap**
75.x: Structural causes: oil (>80% imported) and gold, low export competitiveness, savings-investment gap

75.s: Besides the Stand-By Arrangement, which is a principal IMF lending window for BoP support?
xs: The IMF's BoP lending windows are the **Stand-By Arrangement** and the **Extended Fund Facility**
75.x: The IMF's BoP lending windows are the Stand-By Arrangement and the Extended Fund Facility

75.s: An unconditional IMF drawing right arising from quota subscription is called what?
xs: **Reserve Tranche** = **unconditional drawing right** arising from **quota subscription** and subsequent changes; **RFI** = **rapid financial assistance** for urgent BoP needs.
xa: The Reserve Tranche Position was historically called the **gold tranche**.
75.x: Reserve Tranche = unconditional drawing right arising from quota subscription and subsequent changes; RFI = rapid financial assistance for urgent BoP needs.

75.s: Which IMF facility provides rapid financial assistance for urgent BoP needs?
xs: **Rapid Financing Instrument:** **Rapid financial assistance** through the **IMF** for **urgent balance of payments needs** — **available** to **IMF members**
75.x: Rapid Financing Instrument: Rapid financial assistance through the IMF for urgent balance of payments needs — available to IMF members

75.s: Which IMF facility gives concessional assistance to Low-Income Countries for urgent BoP needs?
xs: **Rapid Credit Facility:** **Concessional assistance** through the **IMF** for **urgent balance of payments needs** — **available** to **low-income countries**
75.x: Rapid Credit Facility: Concessional assistance through the IMF for urgent balance of payments needs — available to low-income countries

75.s: Which additional recommendation was associated with the High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan?
o: A permanently fixed exchange rate determined by the IMF
Replacement of the current account by the capital account
75.x: Along with identifying a sustainable CAD of about 1.6% of GDP, the committee recommended a market-determined exchange rate.
xs: The **Rangarajan Committee** recommended a **market-determined exchange rate** — option **(1)**.
It put a sustainable CAD at about **1.6% of GDP**.
xa: **LERMS** (**1992-93 Budget**): **40%** official / **60%** market.
Unified rate from **1 March 1993**.
Full **current account convertibility** in **August 1994**.
75.tq: Pair the committee with its specific policy recommendation rather than its numerical threshold alone.

75.s: FERA, 1973 was what kind of law?
xs: **FERA 1973** was a **restrictive criminal law** (control of outflow);
75.x: FERA 1973 was a restrictive criminal law (control of outflow);

75.s: FEMA, 1999 is what kind of law?
xs: **FEMA 1999** is a **liberal civil law** (management and regulation)
75.x: FEMA 1999 is a liberal civil law (management and regulation)

75.s: Under LERMS, what share of the exchange rate was at the official rate?
xs: **LERMS** (**1992-93 Budget**) used **40 per cent official rate** and **60 per cent market rate**
75.x: LERMS (1992-93 Budget) used 40 per cent official rate and 60 per cent market rate

75.s: India achieved full current account convertibility in August 1994 by:
o: Setting up the second Tarapore Committee
Accepting Article VIII of the IMF
75.x: Full current account convertibility was achieved in August 1994 when India accepted the obligations under Article VIII of the IMF.
xs: India reached **full current account convertibility in August 1994** by **accepting Article VIII of the IMF** — option **(3)**.
**FEMA** came later (**1999**).
xa: Path: **LERMS** (**1992-93**) → unified rate **1 March 1993** → Article VIII (**1994**).
**Current account convertibility** = free conversion for trade, income and transfers.
Rupee delinked from **sterling** in **September 1975**.
75.tq: Match the convertibility milestone with the specific IMF provision rather than with a domestic statute.

75.s: Freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency for current international transactions is called what?
xs: **current account convertibility** = freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency for **current international transactions**.
xa: **Full current account convertibility** came in **August 1994** (IMF **Article VIII**).
75.x: current account convertibility = freedom to convert domestic currency into foreign currency for current international transactions.

75.s: How many accounts does the IMF's BPM6 use for the Balance of Payments?
xs: The **IMF (BPM6)** uses **three accounts
75.x: The IMF (BPM6) uses three accounts

75.s: Which of the following is NOT ordinarily regarded as a measure for correcting a Balance of Payments deficit?
o: Increasing government spending on domestic projects
75.x: Increasing government spending on domestic projects can raise demand and imports and is therefore not ordinarily treated as a corrective measure in this context. Devaluation, import duties and attracting FDI can help address external imbalance.
xs: **Increasing government spending on domestic projects** is **NOT** a correction tool — it raises demand and imports — option **(3)** (PYQ 2025; APPSC-G2 2025 key).
**Devaluation**, higher **tariffs** and attracting **FDI** are tools used.
xa: Expenditure-reducing policy **cuts** government spending.
**Devaluation** = classic expenditure-switching policy.
**Rangarajan Committee** recommended a **market-determined exchange rate**.
75.tq: Use the demand effect of government spending to eliminate the incorrect correction measure.

75.s: The High Level Committee on Balance of Payments headed by C. Rangarajan during 1991–93 regarded a sustainable current account deficit as approximately
75.x: The C. Rangarajan Committee placed a sustainable CAD at approximately 1.6% of GDP and also recommended a market-determined exchange rate.
xs: The **Rangarajan** High Level Committee on BoP (**1991-93**) put a sustainable CAD at about **1.6% of GDP** — option **(1)**.
It also recommended a **market-determined exchange rate**.
75.tq: Retain the committee-specific threshold and distinguish it from contemporary CAD figures.

76.s: A rise in the rupee's NEER indicates what?
In a fixed exchange-rate system, who fixes the rate?
xs: In a **fixed** system the **government fixes the rate** and **RBI buys/sells** forex to hold it;
76.x: In a fixed system the government fixes the rate and RBI buys/sells forex to hold it;

76.s: In a flexible exchange-rate system, what determines the rate?
xs: In a **flexible** system **demand and supply** set it
76.x: In a flexible system demand and supply set it

76.s: The official lowering of a currency's value under a fixed regime is called what?
xs: Devaluation/revaluation are done by the **government/monetary authority**.
xa: **1991** was India's **last formal devaluation**.
76.x: Devaluation/revaluation are done by the government/monetary authority.

76.s: The official raising of a currency's value under a fixed regime is called what?
xs: Devaluation/revaluation are done by the **government/monetary authority**.
76.x: Devaluation/revaluation are done by the government/monetary authority.

76.s: Depreciation makes repayment of which liabilities costlier?
Large capital inflows tend to cause what to a country's currency?
xs: **Large inflows** raise demand for the domestic currency → **appreciation** (**Dutch disease**).
xa: A **NEER** rise = rupee appreciation → exports less competitive.
76.x: Large inflows raise demand for the domestic currency → appreciation (Dutch disease).

76.s: A system in which the market determines a currency's value is called what?
xs: **Flexible** or **floating exchange rate:** The **market determines** the **currency value**
76.x: Flexible or floating exchange rate: The market determines the currency value

76.s: A market-driven fall in a currency's value is called what?
xs: **Officially increased value** = **revaluation**; **market-driven fall** = **depreciation**.
xa: ⚠ Depreciation/appreciation = market (floating); devaluation/revaluation = government (fixed).
76.x: Officially increased value = revaluation; market-driven fall = depreciation.

76.s: A change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹58 represents what for the rupee?
xs: **$1 = ₹60 → ₹58** = **rupee appreciation**; **$1 = ₹60 → ₹65** = **rupee depreciation**.
xa: **Flexible** rate = **depreciation or appreciation**; **fixed** rate = **devaluation or revaluation**.
Appreciation = fewer rupees per dollar; depreciation = more rupees per dollar.
76.x: $1 = ₹60 → ₹58 = rupee appreciation; $1 = ₹60 → ₹65 = rupee depreciation.

76.s: A change from $1 = ₹60 to $1 = ₹65 represents what for the rupee?
xs: **$1 = ₹60 → ₹58** = **rupee appreciation**; **$1 = ₹60 → ₹65** = **rupee depreciation**.
xa: **Flexible** rate = **depreciation or appreciation**; **fixed** rate = **devaluation or revaluation**.
Appreciation = fewer rupees per dollar; depreciation = more rupees per dollar.
76.x: $1 = ₹60 → ₹58 = rupee appreciation; $1 = ₹60 → ₹65 = rupee depreciation.

76.s: Devaluation or revaluation occurs under which exchange-rate system?
xs: **Flexible** rate = **depreciation or appreciation**; **fixed** rate = **devaluation or revaluation**.
xa: **Bretton Woods (1944)** fixed rates on the dollar.
76.x: Flexible rate = depreciation or appreciation; fixed rate = devaluation or revaluation.

76.s: Under the RBI's convention, a rise in the NEER indicates what for the rupee?
xs: An **increase in NEER** = **rupee appreciation**.
xa: ⚠ Sources differ: other notes say an increase in NEER does not indicate appreciation in their convention.
76.x: An increase in NEER = rupee appreciation.

76.s: A direct exchange-rate quotation expresses:
o: The annual percentage change in the exchange rate
Units of foreign currency per one unit of domestic currency
The number of months of import cover
Units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency
76.x: A direct quote states the amount of domestic currency required for one unit of foreign currency, such as ₹95 = $1.
xs: A **direct quote** gives **units of domestic currency per one unit of foreign currency** (e.g. **₹95 = $1**) — option **(4)**.
Option (2), foreign units per one domestic unit, is the **indirect quote**.
xa: ⚠ Trap: the PYQ's "false" statement **swapped** the direct and indirect quote definitions.
**Import cover** = months of imports that reserves can pay for.
**Exchange rate** = price of one currency in terms of another.
76.tq: Identify the domestic-currency side of the quotation.

76.s: Buying a currency in a market where it is cheaper and simultaneously selling it in another market where it is dearer is known as:
76.x: Arbitrage is the simultaneous purchase of a currency in a cheaper market and its sale in a dearer market (PYQ key). Hedging is covering exchange-rate risk, e.g. through forward contracts; speculation is taking an open position on expected future movements; devaluation is an official lowering of a currency's value under a fixed regime.
xs: **Arbitrage** = buying a currency **cheap in one market** and **selling it dearer in another at the same time** — option **(2)** (PYQ key).
**Hedging** is covering exchange-rate risk (e.g. via forwards); **devaluation** is an official lowering of value under a fixed regime.
xa: **Spot rate** settles **within two days**; **forward rate** is agreed now for a future date.
**Hot currency** = temporary name for a hard currency.
⚠ Arbitrage needs **simultaneous** buying and selling.
76.tq: Arbitrage = same time, two markets, price gap.

76.s: What is the base year of the RBI's NEER index for the rupee?
xs: **NEER** is a **trade-weighted** average against partner currencies, **base 2015-16 = 100**.
76.x: NEER is a trade-weighted average against partner currencies, base 2015-16 = 100.

76.s: Besides the 6-currency index, the RBI publishes a trade-weighted index of how many currencies?
xs: RBI uses **40-currency** and **6-currency** indices
76.x: RBI uses 40-currency and 6-currency indices

76.s: A high REER is generally interpreted as indicating that the rupee is:
o: Convertible only on the capital account
Fixed permanently to the US dollar
76.x: A high REER generally indicates an overvalued rupee. Since REER incorporates relative inflation, it is a better indicator of competitiveness than NEER alone.
xs: A **high REER** means an **overvalued** rupee, which is **less competitive** — option **(1)**.
A **low** REER means an **undervalued** rupee, so option (4) is the reverse.
xa: REER = **NEER adjusted for relative inflation**.
REER is the **better indicator of competitiveness**.
⚠ Deliberate **undervaluation** (as alleged of **China**) = currency manipulation.
76.tq: Apply the index interpretation to the policy meaning of an overvalued currency.

76.s: A managed float is best described as a system in which the exchange rate is:
o: Fixed permanently by a constitutional provision
Determined only by the price of gold
Determined by the market, with central-bank intervention when necessary
Set exclusively by commercial banks without government influence
76.x: In a managed float, market forces determine the rate, while the central bank may intervene directly through forex transactions or indirectly through interest rates.
xs: A **managed float** is **market-set with central-bank intervention** — option **(3)**; it is **India's system**.
Intervention can be **direct** (buy/sell forex) or **indirect** (interest rates).
xa: **Fixed/pegged**: value fixed to a currency, basket or gold; RBI buys/sells to hold it.
**Floating**: market-determined by demand and supply.
India's dual rates were unified into a market-determined rate on **1 March 1993**.
76.tq: Separate market determination from the degree of official intervention.

76.s: In the post-Bretton Woods classification, currency unions and currency boards fall under which regime?
xs: Post-Bretton Woods, **currency unions and currency boards** are **fixed** regimes
xa: **Bretton Woods (1944)**: fixed rates on the dollar.
76.x: Post-Bretton Woods, currency unions and currency boards are fixed regimes

76.s: Under a floating regime, when more units of domestic currency are needed per unit of foreign currency, it is called what?
xs: **depreciation** (floating) = **more** rupees per dollar.
xa: Example: **Rs 80 → Rs 96** per $ = depreciation.
